items.title: 60499_Garvin Bushell oral history interview
items.q: So, we organized this group with his wife playing drums and him playing piano

ctx.x: Sunday night and by Tuesday night I was working with the National Orchestra -- National Band, playing bassoon. They didn't have a decent bassoon player on the Island at that time. But the gimmick was, it only paid $200.00 a month. Mind you, $200.00 a month. But we had some aid. I stayed with my sister-in-law and her husband is one of the important horse trainers there and they had a big house, so they kept the four of us until I got on my feet. So I just turned over my -- when it got to me it was $190.00 a month…

oboe player they didn't have. So, whenever an act came there that they needed a piccolo or oboe or bassoon, why I would go to the various hotels. So I did that for another couple years or so. And I met a trumbone player who was a jazz man from L.A., but he was making his living down there selling encyclopedias. Got rich. And also was a good jazz man. He couldn't read music but he could play. Very big guy -- Bob Smiten. So he introduced me to another fellow who I found out later on was president of Williams…

And sometimes I'd make $150.00 a gig for myself. So, to me it was a good business. And I took on a few pupils too. Private teaching wasn't much because Puerto Ricans weren't in the habit of paying $10.00 a lesson or something.. They could go to the conservatory for a whole season for -- whole semester for $25.00 -- all year. Attend the conservatory -- $25.00. That's all it cost. Government subsidizes the rest of it, I think, through the Ford Foundation and some other benevolent society. And we kept on with this…
